one_liner: Zig CommonMark+GFM parser and HTML/Typst renderer; README shows it ahead of cmark only through a shell-wrapped baseline.
what_it_does: Parses CommonMark 0.31.2 plus the GFM extensions (tables, task lists, strikethrough, extended autolinks, disallowed raw HTML) into a typed AST and renders it to HTML, Typst, Markdown, an ASCII tree, a terminal view or a compact 'AI' dump. It ships as a Zig module, a CLI (`zigmark file.md -o out.html`), a C ABI (`libzigmark.so` with `zigmark_parse`/`zigmark_render_html`) and a WASM build. It also parses and edits YAML/TOML/JSON/ZON frontmatter, edits AST blocks in place, and queries collections of documents. The API is its own, not a cmark drop-in.
how_it_is_fast: Two passes: a first scan of every line collects link reference definitions into a hash map, then a block pass (mecha parser combinators plus hand-written line classifiers over a pre-split line array) and a hand-written inline state machine implement the CommonMark delimiter algorithm. Plain-text runs inside inlines are skipped with a `@Vector` byte-compare scan for the special characters (`*_~[!`<\` and newline, plus `@` under GFM), with a lookup-table scalar tail. Renderers stream into an 8 KiB buffered writer instead of building the output string. Nothing in the code points to a structural advantage over cmark: the README's lead over cmark comes from a harness asymmetry (see gotchas).
when_to_use: Zig projects that want an in-process CommonMark+GFM parser with a typed AST, block mutation and frontmatter editing in one module.
Markdown-to-Typst/PDF pipelines (eisvogel-style preamble driven by frontmatter, mermaid fences rendered to SVG through the lazy pozeiden dependency).
Noncommercial or internal tooling that wants a small static CLI (about 2 MB peak RSS on a 27 KB file) or a WASM build of about 81 KiB.
Doc-site tooling that needs to query or rewrite sections of many Markdown files (the Library query API, --set-block, --section-start/--section-end).
when_not_to_use: Commercial products or paid client work: PolyForm Noncommercial 1.0.0 forbids it without a separate licence from SC2 (solo practitioners using it as a tool are exempted in the README).

When raw conversion speed is the goal: on the repo's own unwrapped comparison lowdown (2.2 ms) beats every zigmark build and discount (2.7 ms) is within one standard deviation of ReleaseFast (2.4 ms); no throughput test on large inputs exists.

Untrusted input without limits: SECURITY.md documents O(n^2) worst-case behaviour of the inline scanner on unmatched brackets, bounded only by the input cap, whereas cmark is built to stay linear on pathological input.
Inputs over 16 MiB: Parser.max_input_bytes defaults to 16 MiB and the CLI uses the default, so larger files fail with error.InputTooLarge.
Toolchains other than Zig 0.16.0 or later; 0.x API that has changed across 11 minor releases since 2025.

integration.dependencies: mecha, zig-clap, mvzr, tomlz and zig-yaml (SC2 forks for the last two); pozeiden (lazy, for mermaid SVG in the CLI/WASM; a no-op fallback when used as a library); commonmark-spec and cmark-gfm are fetched only for the spec tests.
integration.platforms: any Zig target; CI on x86_64-linux and aarch64-linux; wasm32 build; SIMD scan falls back to scalar where no vector length is suggested
integration.thread_safety: not documented (Parser is a plain value struct and all output is caller-owned; pozeiden made its mermaid rendering thread-safe in v0.2.0)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — the CLI takes a file and writes HTML like cmark, but adds -o, enables GFM extensions by default, and the C ABI differs from cmark's cmark_markdown_to_html/node API

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the headline: flake.nix's bench app runs cmark and cmark-gfm through a generated `#!/bin/sh` wrapper (`exec cmark "$@" > /dev/null`) while zigmark, lowdown and discount are spawned directly under `hyperfine -N`, so every cmark run pays an extra shell start on a 2-5 ms start-up-dominated workload (hyperfine's `--output=null` would have made it symmetric), and the cmark peak-RSS rows include the shell. The work also differs: the zigmark CLI parses with GFM extensions on and a mermaid hook, while plain `cmark`/`cmark-gfm` (no -e flags) render CommonMark only.

The README table is stale: it is dated 2026-06-04 (the v0.7.0 release that added the bench app) and says README.md was 27 KB, but README.md is now about 33 KB and the current bench app also writes a 'mermaid-heavy input' table that the README lacks, so the numbers predate releases 0.8.0 to 0.11.1 and the current harness. No CPU or baseline versions are given.

The C ABI (`zigmark_parse`, `zigmark_render_*` in src/root.zig) allocates every AST node and string with `std.heap.page_allocator`, i.e. a page-granular mmap/munmap per allocation, so C callers get a much slower and more memory-hungry path than the CLI's general-purpose allocator; `zigmark_free_string` recovers the length by scanning for the NUL terminator.

The separate `nix run .#benchmark` app (benchmark.md) is a zigmark-only self-comparison whose command `./zig-out/bin/zigmark ./Readme.md > /dev/null` runs under hyperfine -N, so `>` and `/dev/null` are passed as arguments rather than a redirect, and the file name differs in case from README.md.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: rushdown (Rust) is the closer CommonMark sibling and its make-bench numbers beat cmark in-process without a wrapped baseline; pick zigmark only when you need a Zig-native or C-ABI library with Typst output and frontmatter/AST editing, and your use is noncommercial.
verified_claims_summary: One process per run converting the repo's own 27 KB README.md to HTML, hyperfine -N mean over 500 runs on an unstated machine: zigmark ReleaseFast 2.4 ms against cmark 5.3 ms and cmark-gfm 5.6 ms (nixpkgs builds, versions unstated), but the cmark rows include an extra /bin/sh process; the directly spawned C tools lowdown (2.2 ms) and discount (2.7 ms) tie or beat zigmark, so no valid win over C is shown.
status_note: Active (162 commits, v0.11.1 on 2026-08-07, 3 open issues, two of them Zig 0.16 migration bugs in the terminal renderer and spec-runner timing) and passes all 652 CommonMark and 24 GFM spec tests, but PolyForm Noncommercial licensing makes it reference-only for commercial users and the only speed evidence comes from a harness that shell-wraps the cmark baselines.
